setting: A short lecture in an introductory geology class about where volcanoes form.
narrator_intro: Listen to part of a talk in a geology class.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Volcanoes are not randomly scattered across Earth's surface.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Most of them form near the edges of tectonic plates—huge slabs of crust that move slowly over time.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: At divergent boundaries, plates pull apart and magma rises to fill the gap, creating new crust.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: The mid-ocean ridges are a classic example of that process under the sea.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: At convergent boundaries, one plate can sink beneath another in a process called subduction.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Water carried down with the sinking plate helps melt rock above it, feeding chains of volcanoes like those around the Pacific “Ring of Fire.”

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: A smaller number of volcanoes form over hot spots, where a plume of heat rises from deep in the mantle.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: As a plate drifts over a hot spot, a chain of islands can form—Hawaii is the usual classroom example.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: So when you see a volcanic chain on a map, ask first: plate edge or hot spot?

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Next time we'll talk about how magma chemistry changes eruption style—from gentle lava flows to explosive ash columns.

narrator_outro: Now get ready to answer the questions.

questions.narrator_text: What is the talk mainly about?

options.A: How to forecast tomorrow's weather with volcanoes
options.B: Where volcanoes form in relation to tectonic plates and hot spots
options.C: How to build a model volcano for a science fair
options.D: Why oceans have no geological activity

questions.explanation: The professor explains volcanoes at divergent and convergent plate boundaries and over hot spots.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing A—weather forecasting is not the topic.

questions.narrator_text: What happens at divergent boundaries, according to the professor?

options.A: Plates pull apart and magma rises to create new crust

questions.explanation: At divergent boundaries plates pull apart and magma rises to fill the gap, creating new crust.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing B—plates continue to move in the talk's account.

questions.narrator_text: How does subduction help create volcanoes?

options.A: By freezing magma instantly at the surface
options.B: Water carried down with the sinking plate helps melt rock above it
options.C: By removing all oxygen from the atmosphere
options.D: By pushing continents into the Sun

questions.explanation: In subduction, water carried down helps melt rock above the sinking plate, feeding volcanic chains.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing A—that is not the mechanism she describes.

questions.narrator_text: What example does the professor give of a hot-spot chain?
questions.explanation: She says Hawaii is the usual classroom example of a hot-spot island chain.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing A or B—those are not given as hot-spot examples here.
